Niall Johnston, HP CIO September 25, 2026 High-performing organizations have one thing in common: they operate in complex, demanding environments where people need to make fast decisions, collaborate effectively and adapt quickly. Scuderia Ferrari HP needs to be able to make decisions in seconds. Real Madrid C.F. has to engage millions of fans while running a highly complex global operation. Large enterprises, like HP, have to scale AI across a distributed workforce. In each case, technology is no longer just there to keep things running. Used well, it becomes a source of advantage. That was the central theme of a conversation I had with Stefano Maltomini, Head of Digital Transformation at Scuderia Ferrari HP, and Enrique Uriel, Chief Information Officer at Real Madrid C.F, during HP’s C-Suite Summit at the historic Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid recently. Our organizations are very different, but we face similar leadership questions: how to remove friction from work, give people the right tools and experiences, and introduce new capabilities without losing sight of real needs. Start with the problem, not the technology One of the clearest lessons is that technology only provides competitive advantage when it starts with the problem, not the product. With AI moving so quickly, it can be tempting to start with the capability and then look for a use case. Technology leaders must work the other way around: define the need, understand how work happens, and then decide how technology can help. At Scuderia Ferrari HP, engineering and operational teams are enabled to work through complex decisions by deploying specific digital and data capabilities. Real Madrid C.F. deploys secure and connected systems to support the needs of a broad organization spanning employees, athletes, partners, media teams and stadium operations. At HP, helping customers deploy AI at scale means building around clear business outcomes across the full operating environment: people, processes, infrastructure, data and governance. Innovation creates value when it is introduced with purpose and built into the way people actually work. Employee experience is a leadership priority Reliability and efficiency remain essential, but technology leaders also increasingly expect technology to remove friction, improve productivity and help employees do their best work. At Real Madrid C.F., that includes dynamic device catalogues matched to individual roles and AI-powered support that reduces reliance on traditional ticketing systems. At HP, AI is helping identify and resolve workplace issues before they interrupt productivity - from monitoring meeting room technology to addressing support problems before they escalate. This is where the idea of 'invisible' technology matters. When systems work reliably in the background, remove routine friction and help resolve issues before they interrupt work, people can focus on higher-value tasks. Technology connecting people and decisions, faster As work becomes more distributed, organizations need collaboration environments that help people communicate naturally, share context and make decisions wherever they are. The strongest technology strategies balance consistency and scale with enough flexibility to reflect the needs of different teams and roles. The technology leadership mandate The lesson I took from Madrid is that technology supports high-performing organizations when it is grounded in real needs and designed around the people using it. The role of technology leadership is not simply to deploy new capabilities. From the racetrack to the stadium to the workplace, HP’s partnerships show the value of deploying technology with purpose – to remove friction and help people and teams operate at their best, especially in the most complex and demanding environments.
